text: The under-bridge seminar on international affairs ran until two in the morning: the US-China-Russia triangle, lectured by a man who hadn't eaten breakfast in three days.
A fifteen-yuan crash bed in an eight-man dorm—snoring, foot odor, and sleep-talk murmuring 'boss, just one more chance.'
You became the industrial park's last security guard. On both sides of the iron gate, the drifters came and went—you were the only constant.
The camera chose you. Overnight your face hung on a million screens—they called you 'the last of the XX.'
Influencers haul their gear around to film your daily life. More people buy your time than care about you.
Nobody told you the day the hype died. You vanished from the conversation as suddenly as you had appeared in it.
Without a vaccination certificate, you can't even keep your guard shift. Lying in your rented room counting ceiling tiles, by the four hundredth you learned to stop counting.
The phone call about your mother entering the ICU blasted you out of the room you hadn't left in ten years. You want to find a job—your résumé is a blank you can see right through.
'High-paying customer-service jobs in Myanmar, flight included.' You stared at the ad for a long time. Some comments said it was good; others said it was Myawaddy.
Only after arriving did you learn what 'customer service' meant: reciting scripts at gunpoint, beaten for missing your quota. You began studying the one window that faced the sea.
You jumped into the sea. You swam for who knows how long; when a fishing boat hauled you out, you cried like a newborn. Alive—so good.
Your first bet won you three thousand. What you didn't know: the bookmaker lets everyone win their first round.
The umpteenth time of 'I'll quit once I break even.' Your salary card, your credit line, the money borrowed from friends—they all vanished, one by one, in line.
You spent the night in a KFC, salvaging half a burger someone left behind. Your phone still pings match updates; you deleted the app—for the tenth time.
Day thirty at the gambling recovery group. When your turn came, you said: I didn't bet today. The whole room applauded—and so did you, for yourself.
The masseuse at the parlor memorized your birthday, your tastes, and your weak spots. Three months later, your savings vanished along with her WeChat.
A blind-massage parlor pays over ten thousand a month, and national chains fight to hire you. Clients say your hands can see the meridians. You smile: hands are made by practice.
For two years riding on a rich woman's coattails, you earned a hundred thousand a month. The day she turned away, your title, your apartment, and your social circle all reset to zero.
Your boyfriend's spending grew more lavish by the week. Until the day you saw in his trunk the goods no one should ever see—and two pairs of gloves.
An ordinary evening: grocery shopping together, bickering over yogurt brands, sharing one pair of earbuds on the way home. Later, this would be the day you missed most.
The homeless man you once helped finished his first full month on the job and collected his pay. He waved the payslip at you, grinning—like waving a flag.
You passed the abandoned villa complex back in your hometown. The whole village had grown rich making drugs back then; now weeds grow up through living rooms with no roofs.
